target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is educationally valuable and therefore warranted in biology classes.
objection: AG2 argues that the learning goals cited for dissection can be achieved without animal dissection because synthetic models and computer simulations teach biology equally well or better, so dissection is unnecessary.

target: AG1’s assumption that dissection is not tied to animal harm because the animals are already dead or are meat-industry byproducts.
objection: AG2 contends that about 99% of dissection animals are caught in the wild, so dissection is tied to wild capture, which reduces local populations and biodiversity and makes the practice environmentally harmful.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection causes biodiversity loss through wild-capture.
objection: AG1 replies that over 98% of dissected animals were already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, so typical school dissection does not require catching animals in the wild or taking additional lives.

target: AG2’s claim that synthetic models and simulations can replace dissection for the educational gains AG1 cited.
objection: AG1 says that dissection uniquely develops fine motor skills and hand-eye coordination through direct physical manipulation of real tissues, and that models and simulations do not provide those hands-on learning gains to the same extent.

target: AG1’s claim that synthetic models and simulations cannot match dissection’s fine-motor and hand-eye-coordination benefits.
objection: AG2 responds that synthetic anatomical models are designed to be physically handled and manipulated, so they can provide those motor-skill learning gains at least as well as real-animal dissection.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives can match dissection’s critical-thinking benefits.
objection: AG1 argues that real dissection requires students to interpret authentic three-dimensional anatomy, tissue boundaries, and organism-specific variation, which simulations cannot fully reproduce, so alternatives do not provide the same critical-thinking gains.

target: AG1’s claim that only real dissection develops critical thinking in the relevant way.
objection: AG2 says critical thinking in biology labs comes from observing, hypothesizing, and using evidence to make decisions, and those skills can be practiced with synthetic or simulated specimens at least as well as with real dissections.

target: AG2’s environmental objection that dissection is harmful because of landfill waste and specimen disposal.
objection: AG1 argues that when fetal pigs or similar specimens are already landfill-bound byproducts, using them for dissection diverts waste from landfills rather than adding to them, so that aspect of dissection is environmentally preferable rather than harmful.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection depends on wild-caught animals and therefore harms biodiversity.
objection: AG1 says that because most dissected animals are already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts, typical school dissection is not primarily dependent on wild-capture, so biodiversity-loss objections do not apply to that practice.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is typically based on already-dead byproducts rather than wild-caught animals.
objection: AG2 counters that dissection is still largely dependent on wild-capture in practice, and that wild-catching reduces local populations and biodiversity, so the environmental harm remains significant.

target: AG1’s broader justification that dissection should be used because it is educationally useful.
objection: AG2 adds that major standards and training programs do not require animal dissection: AP Biology and the Next Generation Science Standards do not require it, and U.S. and Canadian medical schools do not use animals for physician training. Therefore dissection is not necessary for required educational or medical outcomes.

target: AG2’s claim that the cited standards and medical training show dissection is unnecessary.
objection: AG1 replies that dissection remains a valuable biology teaching practice because it provides distinctive hands-on gains—fine motor skills, hand-eye coordination, and critical thinking—and that typical dissection can use already-deceased byproducts instead of taking additional lives.

target: AG1’s repeated claim that already-dead byproducts remove the main harms of dissection.
objection: AG2 argues that even if some specimens are byproducts, the dissection supply system is still largely based on wild-caught animals, which means the practice remains inhumane and environmentally harmful.

target: AG2’s renewed claim that wild-capture makes typical school dissection environmentally harmful.
objection: AG1 answers that most school specimens are already-dead meat-industry byproducts, so typical dissection can be supplied without catching live animals in the wild and the biodiversity-loss claim does not apply to that setup.

target: AG1’s claim that wild-capture is the main environmental issue.
objection: AG2 introduces a different environmental objection: dissection typically uses chemical preservatives and creates hazardous chemical waste, so it is environmentally harmful even if no wild animals are caught.

target: AG1’s claim that educational value justifies dissection despite other concerns.
objection: AG2 reiterates that AP Biology, the Next Generation Science Standards, and medical training do not require animal dissection, so it is not necessary for the relevant educational outcomes and schools should use non-animal alternatives instead.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is unnecessary because required standards and medical training do not use it.
objection: AG1 responds that dissection still provides unique educational benefits and career motivation, and that when implemented with already-deceased byproduct specimens it is a productive and justified practice rather than an unnecessary one.

target: AG1’s reliance on “already-deceased” specimens to defend dissection.
objection: AG2 says that specimens described as meat-industry byproducts still come from animals raised and slaughtered for meat, so using them does not erase the inhumane and environmental harms tied to the broader animal-supply system.

target: AG2’s claim that byproduct specimens still make dissection harmful because they are part of the meat-industry supply chain.
objection: AG1 argues that because these specimens are already dead and destined for landfills, using them does not require additional raising or slaughter for dissection, removes incremental animal-supply harms, and diverts waste from landfill disposal.
